Measuring the temple; the outer court trampled for 42 months
The two witnesses and their powers
The witnesses killed by the beast; the world rejoices
Resurrection, ascension and earthquake; the survivors give glory to God
The second woe passes
Seventh trumpet: the kingdom proclaimed; the elders' thanksgiving
The heavenly temple opened and the ark of the covenant seen

This is one of the most contested chapters in Revelation, and it carries weight in the debate about the book's date. The measuring of the temple draws on Ezekiel 40-48 (an angel measures an idealised temple) and Zechariah 2:1-5 (Jerusalem measured for protection), while measuring can also mark out for destruction (2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8). Herod's temple had a vast Court of the Gentiles, separated from the inner courts by a balustrade with Greek and Latin warnings forbidding foreigners entry on pain of death (two such inscriptions have been found). Jesus foretold that Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). The period of 42 months, 1,260 days and (in chapter 12) "a time, times and half a time" comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, Daniel's measure for the persecution of the saints, historically associated with Antiochus IV's desecration of the temple (167-164 BC, 1 Maccabees 1-4). It also echoes the three and a half years of drought under Elijah (Luke 4:25; James 5:17).

Partial preterists (notably Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell) argue that a command to measure a still-standing temple implies the book was written before AD 70, and that the 42 months match the Roman campaign from spring 67 to August 70. Most scholars, who date Revelation to about AD 95, reply that John's temple is symbolic (as elsewhere in Revelation, 3:12; 21:22) or that he reuses an older oracle, and that the date question cannot rest on this passage. The two witnesses combine Moses (water to blood, plagues) and Elijah (fire from heaven, shutting the sky), the figures expected at the end in Malachi 4:5 and seen with Jesus on the mountain of transfiguration; early Christian writers (Hippolytus, Tertullian) often identified them as Enoch and Elijah, who never died. The "great city" that is spiritually Sodom and Egypt and where the Lord was crucified invites identification with Jerusalem, though many argue it is Babylon/Rome or the world city. The seventh trumpet then leaps to the consummation, with language from Psalm 2 and Daniel 7, and the ark, lost since the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC and said in 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 to have been hidden by Jeremiah until God gathers his people, appears in the heavenly temple.
A measuring rod like a staff: measure the temple of God, the altar and the worshippers

In Ezekiel 40:3-42:20 a man with a measuring reed measures the future temple, a sign of its restoration and holiness; in Zechariah 2:1-5 Jerusalem is measured as a promise of protection, with God as a wall of fire. Measuring can also mean marking out for judgment (2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Kings 21:13; Amos 7:7-9; Lamentations 2:8). 1 Enoch 61:1-5 has angels take measuring cords to measure the righteous, signifying preservation. Revelation 21:15-17 measures the New Jerusalem.
Surveyors with measuring rods (Greek kalamos, a reed of about 3 metres) laid out cities, temples and land boundaries in the Roman world.
Measuring here most likely signifies protection and ownership: God guards his true sanctuary and worshippers. What exactly the temple, altar and worshippers represent is disputed.

A command concerning the literal Herodian temple still standing when John wrote, separating the faithful remnant (the inner sanctuary, i.e. the true worshippers, the church) from the apostate city given to the Romans (Gentry, Chilton).
A future rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the Tribulation, measured to mark it for God's evaluation and the protection of a believing Jewish remnant (Walvoord, Thomas).
The Reformers' re-establishment of true worship and doctrine, measuring the church by the rule of Scripture and excluding the outer court of nominal (papal) Christendom.
The church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21), spiritually protected even while physically persecuted (Beale, Hendriksen).
The temple of God and the altar

The word naos refers to the inner sanctuary (Holy Place and Holy of Holies), not the whole temple complex (hieron). In Revelation, the naos is usually the heavenly sanctuary (7:15; 11:19; 15:5) and believers are pillars in it (3:12); in the New Jerusalem there is no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22). The altar may be the incense altar of 8:3-5 or the altar of burnt offering under which the martyrs cry (6:9).
Temples (naoi) of the imperial cult stood in Ephesus, Pergamum and Smyrna, the contrast between God's true sanctuary and the emperor's being sharp for Asian readers.
The sanctuary of God's presence, whose identity depends on the interpretive approach. The worshippers being counted suggests that it is people, not merely a building, that God preserves.

Gentry argues the Jerusalem temple was standing, so the book predates AD 70; the inner sanctuary stands for the faithful (Christian) remnant within Israel. Critics reply that the language is visionary and symbolic; Gentry answers that the outer court, the trampled holy city and the echo of Luke 21:24 point to the literal Jerusalem of John's day.
A literal third temple rebuilt in Jerusalem, to be desecrated by the Antichrist (Daniel 9:27; 2 Thessalonians 2:4).
The church, God's spiritual temple, where true worship takes place.
The true, spiritual church as distinguished from the outward ecclesiastical system.
The court outside the temple, given to the nations

Herod's temple had a large outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, where non-Jews could enter; a stone barrier (soreg) with inscriptions forbade them to go further on pain of death (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.2; Antiquities 15.11.5; two inscriptions survive). Ezekiel 44:7-9 condemns bringing foreigners into the sanctuary. Jesus foretold that Jerusalem would be trampled by Gentiles (Luke 21:24).
During the Roman siege in AD 70, rival Jewish factions held the inner temple courts while the Romans eventually burned the outer porticoes and entered the courts (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2-6.4).
The outer court represents what God permits to be overrun or persecuted; the contrast between measured (protected) inner sanctuary and unmeasured (exposed) outer court is the key to interpretation.
The literal outer court and city of Jerusalem, given over to Roman armies (Luke 21:20-24), in contrast to the preserved spiritual remnant.
The literal court of a future temple, given to Gentile domination during the second half of the Tribulation.
The outward visible church overrun by corruption, the papal system "trampling" the church for 1,260 years.
The church's external, physical existence, exposed to persecution, while its inner spiritual life is secure (Beale).
They will trample the holy city

Jerusalem is the holy city (Isaiah 52:1; Nehemiah 11:1; Matthew 4:5). Its trampling by nations is a lament in Isaiah 63:18, Psalm 79:1, Daniel 8:13 (the sanctuary and host trampled under Antiochus) and 1 Maccabees 3:45, 51; 4:60. Luke 21:24 is the nearest parallel.

An image of the people of God, or of their city, under hostile power for a limited time. Elsewhere in Revelation "the holy city" is the New Jerusalem (21:2, 10; 22:19), which suggests to many that here, too, it means God's people rather than the earthly Jerusalem.
Literal Jerusalem, besieged and trampled by Rome in AD 67-70, as Jesus foretold in Luke 21:24.
Literal Jerusalem during the future Tribulation, under the Antichrist's domination.
The church, which suffers persecution throughout the age.
The true church oppressed under papal domination for 1,260 years.
42 months; 1,260 days

Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 limit the persecution of the saints to "a time, times and half a time" (three and a half years); Daniel 9:27 speaks of the covenant broken in the middle of the week; Daniel 12:11-12 has 1,290 and 1,335 days. The period evokes Antiochus IV's persecution and temple desecration (167-164 BC) and Elijah's three-and-a-half-year drought (Luke 4:25; James 5:17). Israel's wilderness journey had 42 stages (Numbers 33). Revelation uses all three forms (11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5).

The time of the church's (or God's people's) persecution and witness, limited by God. Half of seven, it signals a broken, incomplete period of evil. Its relation to Daniel's seventieth week is a major dividing line among views.
The literal period of the Roman war against Judea, from Vespasian's commission in early AD 67 to the fall of the temple in August 70 (about 42 months), as argued by Gentry.
The literal second half (or, for the witnesses, perhaps the first half) of Daniel's seventieth week, a future seven-year Tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
By the year-for-a-day principle, 1,260 years of papal supremacy, variously dated (e.g. 533/538 to 1793/1798, with the French Revolution and Napoleon's capture of Pope Pius VI in 1798 often cited).
The whole period between Christ's first and second comings, during which the church both witnesses and suffers (Beale, Hendriksen).
The 1,260 days fit within the generation ending in AD 70, as in partial preterism, with the seventh trumpet that follows read as the consummation also fulfilled then.
My two witnesses

Valid testimony required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; Numbers 35:30; Matthew 18:16); Jesus sent disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, appear with Jesus at the transfiguration (Mark 9:4), and Jewish tradition expected Elijah's return before the Day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5-6; Sirach 48:10) and a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). Zechariah 4 has two anointed ones (Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor). Qumran anticipated two messiahs, of Aaron and of Israel (1QS 9:11). Early Christian writers often expected Enoch and Elijah to return (Hippolytus, On Christ and Antichrist 43; Tertullian, On the Soul 50).

Prophetic witnesses empowered by God to testify during the period of trampling. The question of whether they are two individuals or a symbol of the witnessing community is central. Their description as lampstands (cf. 1:20, where lampstands are churches) inclines many to the corporate reading.
Two literal individuals in the future Tribulation, often Moses and Elijah (Walvoord leans this way) or Enoch and Elijah, or two prophets in their spirit.

Interpretations vary: the faithful Christian witness in Jerusalem before AD 70 (Chilton, typified by the law and prophets), or particular apostles or leaders (some suggest Peter and Paul, or James the Just and another) killed in that era.

The faithful witnesses against Rome through the 1,260 years of papal dominance, such as the Waldenses, Albigenses, Wycliffe and Hus; their "death" and "resurrection" is applied to the suppression of dissent before the Fifth Lateran Council (1512-1517) and Luther's posting of the theses three and a half years later (Elliott).

The whole church in its prophetic witness (two for legal testimony, and because only two of the seven churches in chapters 2-3 were wholly faithful), suffering and yet vindicated (Beale, Hendriksen, Bauckham).
Clothed in sackcloth

Sackcloth, a coarse dark cloth of goat or camel hair, was worn in mourning and repentance (Genesis 37:34; Jonah 3:5-8; Daniel 9:3; Matthew 11:21). Elijah wore a hairy garment (2 Kings 1:8) and prophets were known by rough garments (Zechariah 13:4; Mark 1:6 for John the Baptist).
The witnesses call for repentance and mourn the sin and coming judgment of those they address; their garb identifies them as prophets in the line of Elijah and John the Baptist.
The two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth

Zechariah 4:2-14 sees a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, interpreted as the "two anointed ones" (literally "sons of oil") who stand by the Lord of the whole earth, namely Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the Davidic governor, who rebuilt the temple "not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:6). In Revelation 1:20 lampstands are churches. Olive oil fuelled the temple menorah (Exodus 27:20).

The witnesses are Spirit-empowered bearers of priestly and royal testimony, like Joshua and Zerubbabel who rebuilt the temple. John adapts one lampstand into two, which supports the view that they represent the witnessing church (lampstands) in its royal-priestly calling (1:6; 5:10).
The church in its kingly and priestly witness, sustained by the Spirit (Beale).
Two individual prophets empowered by the Holy Spirit in the Tribulation.
The witnessing church (or its leaders) as the true priesthood and kingship in contrast to Jerusalem's apostate leaders.
Fire comes from their mouths and consumes their enemies

Elijah called down fire on the soldiers of Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:10-12); God made Jeremiah's words a fire that consumes the people (Jeremiah 5:14); Sirach 48:1-3 says Elijah arose like fire and his word burned like a torch. 4 Ezra 13:10 has the Messiah destroy enemies with a stream of fire from his mouth.

The witnesses' prophetic word carries God's judgment on those who reject it; the fire comes from their mouths, i.e. their testimony. Most see it as figurative (the power of the word), though some futurists take it literally.
Literal miraculous fire defending the witnesses during their ministry.
The power of the gospel word to pronounce judgment on those who oppose it.
Power to shut the sky, turn waters to blood and strike the earth with plagues
Elijah shut the heavens for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; 18:1; Luke 4:25; James 5:17). Moses turned the Nile to blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7:17-20; 1 Samuel 4:8).

The witnesses carry on the ministries of Moses and Elijah: confronting an oppressive and idolatrous power, calling God's people out of bondage and proclaiming judgment. The plagues link them to the trumpet plagues just described.
Literal miraculous powers in the Tribulation; some (Walvoord) see the two as Moses and Elijah themselves.
The church's prophetic witness has power to bring God's judgments, as the trumpets show (Beale).
Figurative of the spiritual power of the faithful witnesses' testimony against the corrupt church.
The beast that comes up from the Abyss will make war on them

The first mention of "the beast", introduced as if already known. It draws on Daniel 7:3, 7 (beasts from the sea) and 7:21, where the little horn wages war against the saints and prevails until the Ancient of Days comes. The Abyss connects it to the demonic origin of 9:1-11; in 17:8 the beast "was, and is not, and is about to come up from the Abyss".

For many scholars the beast's ascent from the Abyss after death reflects the Nero redivivus legend, the belief that Nero would return after his death in AD 68 (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57).
The persecuting power, energised by Satan, which seems to triumph over God's witnesses. It anticipates the fuller portrait of chapters 13 and 17.
Rome under Nero (who persecuted the church and began the Jewish War), or the Jewish authorities allied with Rome; Gentry identifies the beast with Nero/Rome.
The future Antichrist, a world ruler who kills the two witnesses in the middle or end of the Tribulation.
The papacy (or the papal power with its secular allies) suppressing the witnesses.
Satanic persecuting power embodied in states and systems throughout history, culminating before the end.
The great city, spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified

Prophets called Jerusalem "Sodom" when it was unfaithful (Isaiah 1:9-10; Jeremiah 23:14; Ezekiel 16:46-56). Egypt is the archetypal oppressor and place of bondage (Exodus 1-14). Jerusalem killed the prophets (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:33-34), and Jesus was crucified outside its walls (Hebrews 13:12). The adverb pneumatikos ("spiritually", "prophetically", BSB "figuratively") signals a symbolic, Spirit-given name.

The "great city" in Revelation elsewhere always refers to Babylon (16:19; 17:18; 18:10-21), which many identify with Rome. The reference to the crucifixion suggests Jerusalem, so interpreters divide: Jerusalem, Rome, or the world-city of rebellious humanity that includes both. Which city is meant is a disputed matter.

Literal Jerusalem, which killed the Lord and his prophets and is about to be judged (Chilton, Gentry); since Revelation elsewhere calls Babylon "the great city", many partial preterists read "Babylon" in chapters 17-18 as Jerusalem too (an identification that is disputed; see chapter 17).
Literal Jerusalem in the Tribulation, morally degraded and allied with the Antichrist (Walvoord, Thomas).
Papal Rome or the territory of Latin Christendom, spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where Christ was crucified afresh in his members.
The world-city of humanity in rebellion against God (Babylon), which includes Jerusalem's rejection of Jesus; it is everywhere the church suffers (Beale, Bauckham).
Their bodies lie in the street and are not permitted burial

Denial of burial was a supreme disgrace and curse in Israel (Deuteronomy 28:26; Psalm 79:2-3, lamenting the dead of Jerusalem left unburied by the nations; Jeremiah 8:1-2; 16:4). Tobit risked his life to bury executed Jews (Tobit 1:17-19; 2:3-8).

Leaving enemies unburied was a deliberate humiliation in the Greco-Roman world (the Antigone story is the classic example); executed criminals were often denied burial, and crucified bodies were left on crosses.
The world's utmost contempt for the witnesses: total public humiliation, exposed to "peoples, tribes, languages and nations" (11:9), which points beyond a single local event to a universal scene.
A literal public display, which some futurists suggest would be visible worldwide through modern media.
The apparent defeat and public shaming of the church at the end of the age.
Three and a half days

A brief counterpart to the 1,260 days of witness: the witnesses' public ministry lasts three and a half years, their apparent defeat three and a half days. It recalls Jesus' death and resurrection after three days and Daniel's half-week.
A short time of apparent triumph for evil, contrasted with the longer period of witness; the death of the witnesses is real but brief, and vindication follows.

Three and a half years, by the day-year principle, from the Fifth Lateran Council's declaration of victory over dissent (May 1514) to Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (October 1517), a match Elliott emphasized.
A literal three and a half days.
A short period of apparent triumph over the church immediately before Christ's return.
Those who dwell on the earth gloat, celebrate and send one another gifts

An inverted Purim: in Esther 9:19, 22 the Jews celebrated deliverance from their enemies by sending portions to one another; here the persecutors celebrate the death of God's witnesses. Compare also Nehemiah 8:10-12.
Gift exchange marked Roman festivals such as the Saturnalia and imperial celebrations of victories.

The world's relief at being freed from the prophets' unwelcome testimony ("these two prophets had tormented them"), a parody of godly celebration. It shows how deeply the message of repentance was resented.
The breath of life from God entered them and they stood on their feet
Ezekiel 37:5, 10: in the valley of dry bones, breath enters the slain and they stand on their feet, a vision of Israel's national restoration. Genesis 2:7 has God breathe life into Adam.

The vindication and resurrection of the witnesses. Whether this is a literal bodily resurrection of two individuals, the final resurrection of the church, or a figure for the revival of the church's witness depends on the overall approach.
Literal resurrection and ascension of the two witnesses near the end of the Tribulation.
The revival of Protestant witness at the Reformation, or later restoration of liberty to Protestants.
The vindication of the church at Christ's return (the resurrection of the righteous), or more generally God's pattern of reviving his witness after apparent defeat.
The vindication of the martyred witnesses and the church's triumph over Jerusalem, sometimes linked to the safety of the church after the city's fall.
"Come up here" — they went up to heaven in a cloud

Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11); Jewish tradition held that Moses too was taken up (the lost Assumption of Moses; Josephus, Antiquities 4.326 says a cloud came over him). Jesus ascended in a cloud (Acts 1:9-11). John himself heard "Come up here" in Revelation 4:1.

Public vindication: the enemies see the witnesses honoured by God, as Jesus' enemies will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds (1:7). The witnesses follow the pattern of their Lord: witness, death, resurrection, ascension.

A literal ascension of the two witnesses; some (e.g. some mid-tribulationists) connect it with a rapture of believers, but most dispensationalists place the rapture before the Tribulation (Revelation 4:1 is often read as its symbol).
The church's exaltation at the end, possibly corresponding to 1 Thessalonians 4:17.
A great earthquake: a tenth of the city fell, seven thousand killed

Ezekiel 38:19-20 has a great earthquake in the land at God's final judgment; Amos 5:3 says a city that marches out a thousand will be left with a hundred (a tenth). Elijah was told that God kept 7,000 who had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18), so the number reverses Elijah's remnant: now 7,000 die and the majority are converted.
Earthquakes repeatedly destroyed cities in Asia Minor (Sardis AD 17; Laodicea c. AD 60).

A limited judgment (a tenth, not a third or all) that, unlike the trumpets, results in the majority repenting. Bauckham argues this is the key reversal of the book: where judgment alone failed (9:20-21), the witness of the church, vindicated by God, leads the nations to give glory to God.

Upheaval in Jerusalem in the war years; some note Josephus's report of an earthquake and storm in AD 68 (Jewish War 4.4.5). Interpreters differ on whether the survivors' response is genuine conversion.
A literal earthquake in Jerusalem near the end of the Tribulation.
The political upheaval of the Reformation era or the French Revolution, in which a "tenth" kingdom of the papal realm fell (often France).
A partial judgment that, with the church's vindicated witness, brings many to repentance.
The rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven

"Give glory to God" can be a call to confession and repentance (Joshua 7:19; Jeremiah 13:16), and in Revelation it is the response of repentance (14:7; 16:9, where the lack of it is condemned). "God of heaven" is a Persian-era title in Daniel 2:18-19, 37, 44, Ezra and Nehemiah, used by Gentile kings who acknowledge Israel's God (Daniel 4:34-37).

Whether this is genuine conversion or merely forced acknowledgment is disputed. Bauckham, Caird and others argue for true repentance, since 14:7 and 16:9 equate "giving glory" with repentance; Beale, Thomas and others think it may be coerced recognition, like Nebuchadnezzar's.
Bauckham and Sweet: a picture of the conversion of the nations through the church's faithful witness, the great hope of Revelation.
Thomas and Walvoord: likely the conversion of a remnant in Jerusalem, perhaps connected with the salvation of Israel (Romans 11:26), though some say it is only fearful acknowledgment.
Varies: either superficial fear in Jerusalem, or the conversion of many Jews who acknowledged Christ after the judgments.
The second woe has passed; the third woe is coming soon
Continues the woe-oracle structure of 8:13 and 9:12.

Ties the interlude (10:1-11:13) to the sixth trumpet. The third woe is not explicitly identified; most link it to the seventh trumpet and the judgments it opens, including the devil's rage on the earth (12:12) and the bowls (15-16).
The seventh trumpet: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ

Psalm 2:2 speaks of the Lord and his anointed (Christ), against whom the nations rage; Daniel 2:44 and 7:14, 18, 27 promise an everlasting kingdom given to the Son of Man and the saints; Exodus 15:18 ends the song of the sea with the Lord reigning forever; Obadiah 21 and Zechariah 14:9 foresee the Lord as king over all the earth. Trumpets were sounded at royal enthronements (1 Kings 1:34, 39; 2 Kings 9:13).

Emperors claimed kingship over the oikoumene, the inhabited world; coins and inscriptions proclaimed Caesar's reign as a gift of the gods. The heavenly announcement asserts that world rule belongs to God and his Messiah.

The climax of the trumpets and of the mystery of God (10:7). The singular "kingdom" stresses that world rule passes entirely to God and Christ. The nature and timing of this transfer is the central millennial question in this chapter.
The decisive transfer of the kingdom at Christ's ascension and its public vindication in AD 70, after which the kingdom grows through the church until the final consummation (Gentry, Chilton).
Anticipates Christ's literal return and earthly reign; dispensationalists see the reign beginning at the second coming after the Tribulation, followed by the millennium (Walvoord).
The final establishment of Christ's kingdom after the overthrow of the papal and Turkish powers, the goal toward which the whole prophetic history of the trumpets has moved (Elliott, Barnes).
The consummation of the kingdom at Christ's return at the end of history (Beale, Hendriksen); the seventh trumpet parallels the seventh seal and bowl.

The full arrival of the kingdom and the "last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52) in AD 70. This places the view outside creedal orthodoxy, since the creeds confess a future return and bodily resurrection; proponents argue that the New Testament's time statements require it.
The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and give thanks

The elders recall the twenty-four priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:7-19) and the elders of Israel before God (Isaiah 24:23); their prostration and hymn follow temple patterns of thanksgiving (todah). "Lord God Almighty" (Pantokrator) renders the Septuagint's title for the Lord of hosts (Amos 4:13).
Prostration (proskynesis) before rulers was a feature of eastern and later imperial court ceremony; Domitian reportedly liked to be addressed as "Lord and God" (Suetonius, Domitian 13).
The heavenly court responds to the kingdom proclamation with thanksgiving, affirming that God has taken his great power and begun to reign.
The one who is and who was (no longer "who is to come")

The threefold title of 1:4, 8 and 4:8 (who was, and is, and is to come) echoes Exodus 3:14 as expanded in Jewish tradition; the Palestinian Targum (Pseudo-Jonathan) on Deuteronomy 32:39 and Exodus 3:14 develops a similar three-tense formula (a later text, reflecting earlier traditions).
Greek religious formulas spoke of Zeus who was, is and will be (Pausanias 10.12.10), which Revelation adapts for Israel's God.

The omission of "who is to come" here and in 16:5 is deliberate: from the perspective of the seventh trumpet, God has come and begun to reign. It signals that the seventh trumpet depicts the consummation.
God's "coming" in judgment in AD 70 established his reign in a decisive new way, while a final coming remains (for partial preterists) future.
Anticipates the second coming at the end of the Tribulation.
The final coming of God at the end of history (Beale, Bauckham).
The nations raged, your wrath came; the time to judge the dead and reward your servants

Psalm 2:1, 5, 12 (the nations rage and God speaks in wrath) and Psalm 99:1 in the Greek translation (the Lord reigns, let the peoples be angry). Daniel 12:2 speaks of the resurrection of the dead for judgment and reward; Psalm 115:13 blesses those who fear the Lord, small and great. Amos 3:7 calls the prophets God's servants.

A summary of the final events: the nations' rebellion, God's wrath, the judgment of the dead, and the reward of prophets, saints and God-fearers. It previews chapters 19-20, especially the last judgment (20:11-15).

Most postmillennialists (and partial preterists) take 11:18 as a proleptic summary of the final judgment at the end of history, after the kingdom has grown through the gospel; some partial preterists see a first-century foreshadowing in AD 70.
The final judgment at Christ's single return, parallel to Revelation 20:11-15, supporting the recapitulation structure of the book.

The judgment of the dead mentioned here is anticipatory; the rewards are given at various stages (at the judgment seat of Christ, after the Tribulation, and the great white throne after the millennium).
Anticipates both the rewards at Christ's return and, after the millennium, the final judgment, summarised together.

The judgment of the dead took place in the spiritual realm in AD 70 (Max King, Don Preston); critics say this denies the future judgment of the creeds, while proponents reply that the New Testament places that judgment within the first-century generation and that creeds are subordinate to Scripture.
To destroy those who destroy the earth

A wordplay on diaphtheirō (ruin, corrupt). Genesis 6:11-13 (in the Greek translation) says the earth was corrupted and God would destroy it with the corrupters; Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a "destroying mountain" that corrupts the whole earth. Jubilees and 1 Enoch associate the watchers' corruption of the earth with the flood judgment.
Imperial propaganda presented Rome as the bringer of peace and prosperity (Pax Romana); Revelation inverts this, calling Rome (Babylon) the corrupter of the earth (19:2).

God's judgment is fitting retribution (lex talionis) on those who ruin his creation and its peoples, especially the beast and Babylon (19:2). It affirms God's commitment to his creation rather than its abandonment.
God's temple in heaven opened and the ark of his covenant seen

The ark, symbol of God's presence and covenant, kept in the Holy of Holies (Exodus 25:10-22; Leviticus 16:2), disappeared at the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC; the Second Temple's Holy of Holies was empty (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.5; Pompey found it so in 63 BC, Tacitus, Histories 5.9). 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 relates that Jeremiah hid the ark until God would gather his people again, and 2 Baruch 6:7-10 has an angel hide the temple vessels until the restoration. Jeremiah 3:16 says that in the future the ark will no longer be remembered.
